**Before the visit**
- Add the appointment date on the Visit tab. MenoMap shows how ready your notes are and what would make them more complete.
- Choose the topics and questions that matter most to you. Keep it to three or four.
- Create notes for the last 30 or 90 days. Check that your medication list is up to date.

**During the visit**
- Hand over or show the first page. It is designed to be read in under a minute: numbers, averages, the heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the notes in that language.

**What the notes are and are not**

They are a summary of what you entered, plus anything you chose to import from the Health app. They are not a diagnosis or complete medical records, and all patterns in them are coincidence checks, not proof of cause. Your doctor may ask questions the notes cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the visit**

Add every new medication with its start date. In a few weeks MenoMap can show your entries before and after, which makes the next check-up easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day that completes 12 months in a row without a period, when this is not explained by something else (such as pregnancy, some medications or surgery). In many countries it happens on average in the early fifties, but it is common at any time from the mid-forties to the mid-fifties.

**Perimenopause** is the period of several years leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall unevenly, so periods can become irregular, heavier, lighter, more frequent or less frequent. Many changes people associate with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, changes in sleep and mood, often begin then, while periods are still continuing. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably longer and looks different for each person.

**Postmenopause** is everything after that 12-month boundary. Some symptoms settle over time; others can last for years.

Menopause can also happen earlier because of surgery that removes the ovaries, some forms of cancer treatment or other health conditions. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency and is worth discussing with a doctor.

**How it is recognised.** In many people over 45, doctors recognise perimenopause or menopause based on your medical history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed because hormone levels vary from day to day. They are used more often when the person is younger or the picture is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is keep an honest record of what you notice: hot flashes, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, often in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with redness, sweating, a racing heart or a chill afterwards. Night sweats are the same thing during sleep and can be strong enough to wake you or soak the bedding.

They are among the most common changes around menopause. Some people have a few mild ones; others have many a day, so they disrupt work and sleep. In some they go away within a few years; in others they last much longer.

**What can make them more likely.** People often notice patterns with alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, warm rooms, stress or heavy bedding. This varies greatly from person to person, so tracking your own tags can be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes too.** Flushing and sweating can also be caused by thyroid problems, infections, some medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not match the usual pattern or are accompanied by weight loss, fever or feeling generally unwell, mention it to your doctor.

**How to describe them well.** Useful information for a visit:
- Roughly how many there are by day and how many by night
- How strong they are and how long they last
- What they interrupt: sleep, work, conversations, exercise
- What seems to come before them
- What you have tried and whether it changed anything

The Hot Flash button and logging afterwards in MenoMap exist precisely so you can record all this without much effort.

**Help is available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, as well as practical approaches. Which suit you is a question for a conversation with your doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT, hormone replacement therapy, or MHT) replaces part of the estrogen that the body produces in smaller amounts around menopause. Major guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats for many people, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**It comes in different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal preparations for local symptoms such as dryness. People who still have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen along with estrogen to protect the lining of the uterus.

**Benefits and risks depend on the person:** on age, time since periods stopped, personal and family medical history (for example breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease) and on the type and way of administering the treatment. That is why it is a decision to be made with a doctor who knows your medical history, and not something the app can decide.

**Questions people often ask:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me and why or why not?
- Which type and form would you suggest and why?
- What benefits can I expect and how quickly?
- What are my personal risks and how do they compare with not treating?
- What should I watch for and when should we reassess it?

**If you already take it,** record it in MenoMap (Profile → Medications). MenoMap will show your hot flashes before and after you started, as a coincidence check, not proof, so that at the check-up you have something concrete to discuss.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not suitable for everyone, and some people simply prefer to choose other paths. There are several.

**Prescription medications.** For some non-hormonal medications there is evidence that they reduce hot flashes. Among them are certain medications originally developed for other conditions and a newer group of medications developed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking therapies and mind-body approaches.** For cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted to menopause there is evidence that it makes hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome and improves sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes that help people:**
- Layers of clothing that you can quickly remove
- A fan on the desk and by the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Noticing and easing personal triggers (tags and experiments in MenoMap help here)
- Regular physical activity and a steady sleep routine

**Dietary supplements and herbal preparations.** The evidence for many of them is uneven or limited, quality varies, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including over-the-counter products.

**Try one change at a time.** Two-week experiments in MenoMap compare your own entries before and during a change, which is easier to judge than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most appointments are short and it is hard to recall on the spot all the nights of the past month. People usually remember the most recent or the worst days. A simple record fills that gap.

**What a diary gives your doctor:**
- How often symptoms occur and how strong they are, not just that they occur
- Whether things are improving, getting worse or staying the same
- What was happening around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medications
- A starting point for comparison if you try some treatment

**Keep it simple.** A diary helps only if you keep it. MenoMap is built around a one-tap Hot Flash button and a four-question evening entry, so it takes a few seconds and you do not need a notebook.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Two to four weeks of entries usually show a clearer picture than one bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid and anything that worries you. The Visit tab in MenoMap helps you choose questions and prints them alongside your notes.

backTranslations.479:
After 12 months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding should be checked by a doctor**, even if it happened only once and even if it was only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Most often the cause turns out not to be serious. Thinning of the lining of the vagina or uterus, for example, is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat when found early. That is why public health guidelines say it should be examined rather than waited on.

**If you take hormone therapy,** some bleeding patterns can be expected, depending on the type you take. Bleeding that is unexpected for your treatment, heavier than usual or occurring at the wrong time should also be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or health service and say that you have had bleeding after menopause.
- Note the date, the amount and anything else you noticed. MenoMap can keep this for you (Profile → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding occurred. It will remind you to have it checked and will include it in the visit notes.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints in middle age and rarely has just one cause.

**Night sweats** can wake you directly or leave you too hot or too damp afterwards to fall asleep again.

**Other common factors:**
- The need to urinate at night
- Anxiety or racing thoughts
- Alcohol, which can help you fall asleep but usually disrupts the second half of the night
- Caffeine later in the day
- Pain, restless legs or a partner's snoring
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which can be a sign of sleep apnoea (worth mentioning, especially if you are very sleepy during the day)

**What usually helps people.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and layers of clothing you can remove; a steady wake-up time; and less alcohol before bed. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured and well-researched approach, and many doctors can refer you to it.

**What to track.** For a week or two log a sleep rating, night hot flashes, alcohol and late caffeine. The evening entry and hot flash logging in MenoMap do this in a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can display your sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside your night sweats, as context, not as an explanation.

**When to see a doctor.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example, when driving), mood or daily life, or if you notice pauses in breathing or gasping for air at night.
